sentences.text: Provisions were $1.1 billion, compared to $1.3 billion in the prior year, largely driven by a smaller ACL build for transfer risk associated with exposures outside the U.S., driven by safety and soundness considerations under U.S. banking law, partially offset by a 7% increase in net credit losses, primarily driven by the ongoing normalization from post-pandemic lows in Mexico Consumer.
The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion for 2024 compared to 2023.

The provision for credit losses for 2024 was primarily driven by credit card as well as small business loan growth, and asset quality deterioration in the commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.

comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures detail the Provision for Credit Losses for 2024. GS reports a provision of $1.54 billion, an increase from $1.14 billion in 2023, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio. C reports a provision of $1.1 billion, a decrease from $1.3 billion in 2023, driven by a smaller ACL build for non-U.S. transfer risk and a 7% increase in net credit losses primarily from Mexico Consumer normalization. While both highlight credit card charge-offs (GS explicitly) and credit normalization (C explicitly) as key factors, GS's provision is driven by card charge-offs specifically, whereas C's provision reflects a mix of ACL build reductions and card/consumer normalization.

comparisons.peer_topic: Provision for Credit Losses and Allowance Metrics
comparisons.peer_summary: The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion (up from $9.3 billion prior year), reflecting $8.6 billion in net charge-offs driven by Card Services and a $2.0 billion net addition to the allowance, which totaled $26.9 billion at year-end.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM disclose their Provision for Credit Losses and the composition of net charge-offs and allowance builds for 2024. JPM reports a provision of $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion in net charge-offs driven by Card Services and a $2.0 billion net addition to the allowance. C reports a provision of $1.1 billion, driven by a smaller ACL build for transfer risk and a 7% increase in net credit losses primarily from Mexico Consumer. Both identify 'credit normalization' or 'seasoning' in consumer/card portfolios as a driver of charge-offs, but JPM's scale is significantly larger, and C's provision is offset by a reduction in the ACL build for non-U.S. risks, which is not a factor mentioned in JPM's consolidated summary.

sentences.text: Provisions were $1.1 billion, compared to $1.3 billion in the prior year, largely driven by a smaller ACL build for transfer risk associated with exposures outside the U.S., driven by safety and soundness considerations under U.S. banking law, partially offset by a 7% increase in net credit losses, primarily driven by the ongoing normalization from post-pandemic lows in Mexico Consumer.

• The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion of net charge-offs and a net addition to the allowance for credit losses of $2.0 billion. Net charge-offs increased by $2.4 billion, driven by Card Services, reflecting the seasoning of vintages originated in recent years, credit normalization, and balance growth. The net addition to the allowance for credit losses included a net addition of $2.1 billion in consumer, driven by Card Services, and a net reduction of $19 million in wholesale.
The provision in the prior year was $9.3 billion, reflecting $6.2 billion of net charge-offs and a $3.1 billion net addition to the allowance for credit losses.
